description: This event is in-person only, but open to all. To receive the calendar invite, email Julia Wu (Julia.Wu@ucsf.edu) Contemporary mindfulness programs have demonstrated benefits for health and well-being, yet their application within Indigenous communities requires attention to cultural context, historical trauma, and Indigenous ways of knowing. This presentation introduces IndigenousMIND, a community-engaged framework that integrates evidence-based mindfulness approaches with Indigenous cultural practices, including storytelling, ceremony, traditional arts, and relationships with land and community. Drawing on research and collaborations with Indigenous Nations, Dr. Proulx will discuss lessons learned in adapting mindfulness interventions, emerging findings related to stress and cardiovascular health, and opportunities for culturally grounded approaches to integrative health and healing. Jeffrey Proulx, PhD, is a Haudenosaunee (Six Nations) scholar, researcher, and educator whose work focuses on culturally grounded mindfulness interventions andhealth equity in underserved communities. He is adjunct faculty at Brown University, where he has held appointments in Psychiatry and Human Behavior, Behavioral and Social Sciences, and Contemplative Studies. He is also Vice President and co-founder of the Indigenous Mindfulness Coalition, an Indigenous-led nonprofit dedicated to supporting Indigenous well-being through contemplative practices, cultural revitalization, research, and community engagement. Dr. Proulx developed the IndigenousMIND framework, which brings together contemporary mindfulness approaches with Indigenous cultural practices, values, and ways of knowing. His research, supported by the National Institutes of Health and private foundations, explores the potential of culturally adapted mindfulness interventions to address stress, hypertension, intergenerational trauma, and other health disparities. He is also co-editor of Beyond White Mindfulness: Critical Perspectives on Racism, Well-Being, and Liberation (Routledge, 2022). The Osher Center for Integrative Health hosts monthly research seminars that are open to the research and clinical community at large. Seminars are held from September to June and are generally virtual. Presentations cover a wide range of topics relating to integrative health, many with a focus on integrative health equity. Research Seminars are organized by Ariana Thompson-Lastad, PhD and Joanne Qina’au, PhD, MA, E-YT750. Please contact Julia Wu (julia.wu@ucsf.edu) with any questions., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform

description: Value-Based Care: What It Is, Why It Matters, and What It Means for UCSF Value-based care is reshaping how health systems deliver, measure, and improve care, with a growing emphasis on outcomes and patient experience. This Grand Rounds will examine how value-based care models advance the quintuple aim of improving quality, reducing costs, enhancing patient and clinician experiences, and promoting health equity. The session will explore how quality measures, health care utilization, and risk adjustment influence performance in alternative payment models, highlighting the essential role of population health in UCSF’s Clinical Enterprise Plan. Speaker: Timothy Judson, MD, MPH, is an associate professor of medicine at UCSF in the Division of Hospital Medicine at UCSF Health and the Division of Clinical Informatics and Digital Transformation (DoC-IT). He is also interim chief population health officer at UCSF Health and chief clinical and innovation officer at Canopy Health, where he oversees health care quality and value. Judson previously served as medical director of care delivery transformation in the Office of Population Health and medical co-director of adult care transitions at UCSF Health. description: Making Health Promotion Meaningful: Community-engaged Strategies for Reaching Diverse Priority Populations Presented by Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH, is an associate professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and serves as director of the NYU Center for the Study of Asian American Health. She is nationally recognized for her expertise in community-based participatory research (CBPR) and health equity initiatives aimed at reducing health disparities in immigrant and minority populations. Dr. Kwon’s research focuses on chronic disease prevention, cultural competency in healthcare, and the social determinants of health. She has led multiple NIH-funded projects addressing health issues in underserved communities, with a particular focus on Asian American populations. As a leader in public health, Dr. Kwon collaborates with community-based organizations to design and implement culturally tailored interventions. Her work highlights the importance of building trust and partnerships between healthcare systems and the communities they serve. She has published extensively on CBPR methodologies and health equity frameworks. Dr. Kwon is committed to advancing inclusive and equitable approaches to improving health outcomes across diverse populations. Learning Objectives: At the end of this activity, learners will be able to: Apply key principles of social marketing and cultural adaptation that can inform efforts to close gaps between current and ideal practice in health promotion and disease prevention for reaching priority populations. Describe how community engagement, participatory approaches, and cultural relevance can support more whole-person, integrated care through clinical practice, research, and education for diverse priority populations. Identify broad strategies for adapting evidence-based health programs to improve relevance, implementation, and sustainability in priority communities, with the goal of improving health outcomes. All relevant financial relationships have been mitigated prior to the commencement of the activity. This CME activity meets the requirements under California Assembly 1195, continuing education, and cultural and linguistic competency. description: The Academic Senate is pleased to announce the selection of Margot Kushel MD, as the recipient of the Fourth Annual Faculty Research Lectureship in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences for her groundbreaking research on homelessness, housing instability, health, and the translation of evidence into policy and systems change. The lecture, titled “Housing, Homelessness, and Health: Bringing Evidence to the Policy Discussion.” will take place on Thursday, December 10, from 3:30pm – 5:00pm at Rock Hall, 1550 4th St., on Mission Bay Campus, with a small reception to follow. The lecture will also be broadcast on Zoom. Dr. Kushel is an internationally recognized leader in health services research whose work has advanced understanding of the causes and consequences of homelessness, the relationship between housing and health, and evidence-based approaches to preventing and ending homelessness. Her work combines rigorous research with community engagement and policy translation, with particular attention to older adults and other populations experiencing structural marginalization. Over the course of her career, she has authored nearly 200 peer-reviewed publications and has served as principal investigator or co-investigator on numerous federally funded studies. A defining feature of Dr. Kushel’s work is its direct connection to policy and practice. In 2019, she established the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative (BHHI) with a $30 million gift from Marc and Lynne Benioff, bringing together researchers, people who experienced homelessness, policymakers, service providers, and community organizations to translate findings into action. She is also principal investigator of the California Statewide Study of People Experiencing Homelessness (CASPEH), the most comprehensive study of homelessness in California in decades. The study surveyed a representative sample of 3,200 adults across the state, and its findings have informed policymakers and helped reshape public understanding of homelessness and its potential solutions. Dr. Kushel has also led pioneering research on older adults experiencing homelessness through the National Institute on Aging-funded Health Outcomes of People Experiencing Homelessness in Older Middle Age (HOPE HOME) study. Since 2012, the study has generated important findings on functional decline, social isolation, health care utilization, mortality, and the “graying” of the homeless population, while informing legislation and national policy discussions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Kushel helped develop and implement responses for people experiencing homelessness, including Project Roomkey, testing and vaccination efforts, and shelter-based public health protocols. Margot Kushel, MD, is Professor of Medicine and Division Chief of the Division of Health and Society in the UCSF Department of Medicine at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital and Trauma Center. She is Director of the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative and the UCSF Action Research Center for Health. She also maintains an active internal medicine practice at the Richard Fine People’s Clinic at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital, caring for patients with complex medical and social needs. The Fourth Annual Faculty Research Lecture in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences will be held on Thursday, December 10, from 3:30pm – 5:00pm at Rock Hall, 1550 4th St., on Mission Bay Campus and will be broadcast on Zoom. The Faculty Research Lecture in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences award was established in 2023. This award is bestowed on an individual member of the UCSF faculty with outstanding achievements in social, behavioral, and health policy research. UCSF faculty are asked to consider the outstanding research contributions of their colleagues and submit nominations for this prestigious award to the Academic Senate Committee on Research.
